questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A note whose deadline meets a timetable
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a note's deadline binds despite a closed road
questions.stem: Sheet 11 of the projection records that the note must be delivered before the spring timetable closes, though the road over which it would travel is closed for repairs until the same date.

options.text: The deadline is stated in the terms of the note and binds whoever receives it, timetable or not.
The deadline cannot bind, since the road being shut makes delivery physically impossible.
options.misconception: assumes physical impossibility cancels an obligation

options.text: The deadline binds only the messenger, since the road works are the cause of any delay.
options.misconception: puts the obligation on the carrier alone

options.text: The deadline is void, since no note may fix a date that the season makes doubtful.
options.misconception: treats seasonal doubt as voiding the term

questions.explanation: A note that names a deadline fixes it, and those who made it are bound whatever the road does. Difficulty may excuse delay; it does not remove the term or transfer it to the messenger.
questions.hint: Ask who made the note and who is bound.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose a blockade is built to serve
questions.stem: Sheet 12 carries a note explaining what a blockade is designed to achieve rather than what it achieves at once.

answer.exemplar: A blockade is not a way to seize territory; it is a way to interrupt supply. By closing the approaches to a port or a coast, the blockading power seeks to make the supply of food, arms and money to the other side difficult enough that its government must stop the acts that provoked the blockade, or accept terms it would otherwise refuse. Its immediate aim is pressure, not possession.

questions.explanation: A blockade works by interrupting supply so the other side is forced to yield, not by taking ground. Reading it as an attempt to seize territory, or as effective only when complete, misreads it.
questions.hint: Ask what the blockade puts pressure on.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Troops in a capital that has declared a republic
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of foreign troops on a new proclamation

stimulus.body: The dispatch records that a detachment of the neighbouring army entered the capital on the morning of the proclamation and that the proclamation declaring a republic had been read from the steps of the council house the previous evening. It adds that the detachment was ordered to hold the barracks and the treasury and that no orders were issued against the council.

questions.stem: Sheet 13 in this projection asks whether the troops' presence affects the republic's standing.

options.text: No, because troops in a capital are a fact of the ground and never touch the standing of a state.
options.misconception: treats presence as legally irrelevant

options.text: Yes, because foreign troops present in a capital at the moment of a proclamation may be read as recognition.
No, because the dispatch says the troops were ordered to hold barracks and never touched the council.
options.misconception: treats restraint as proof of neutrality

options.text: Yes, because the republic ceases to exist once any foreign soldier stands on its soil.
options.misconception: claims any foreign presence dissolves a state

questions.explanation: A proclamation is a claim, and another state's troops in the capital at that moment may be read as that state standing behind the new regime. Restraint does not remove the meaning of the presence.
questions.hint: Ask what the presence can be read as.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: Say what reopening an article within a sitting produces

stimulus.body: The minutes record that the assembly adopted a set of preliminary terms on the first day, that on the fourth day it reopened the second article, and that the reopened article was adopted in an amended form before the sitting closed. A note in the margin states that no party objected to the reopening while the sitting was still open.

questions.stem: Sheet 14 asks the team to say what the minutes show about the settlement's terms.

options.text: That the original terms stood unchanged, since nothing in the minutes records a final vote.
options.misconception: infers finality from the absence of a vote

options.text: That the second article was void, because reopening a settled article is forbidden.
options.misconception: assumes reopening is always forbidden

options.text: That the terms were revised while the sitting remained open, and the later article is the operative one.
That the conference became two assemblies, since a reopened article divides the parties.
options.misconception: reads reopening as splitting the body

questions.explanation: Terms adopted while a sitting remains open may be reopened and re-adopted, and the minutes show this with no objection taken. No recorded final vote says nothing about finality.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sitting was still open.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Build an account of how exceptions can create a duty
questions.stem: Sheet 15 asks the team to build a short account of how a list of exceptions can create a duty rather than remove one.

options.text: By naming who is released, since a list of exceptions shows the scope of what remains owed.
options.misconception: reads an exception list as a limit on the duty

options.text: By showing the whole rule, since exceptions are how a rule states its own extent.
options.misconception: treats exceptions as mere explanatory detail

options.text: By shifting the burden, since an exception always places the duty on the exempt party.
options.misconception: assumes exemption transfers the burden

options.text: By making the rest of the rule bite harder, since each carve-out shows how seriously the remainder applies.

questions.explanation: A list of exceptions shows where the rule does not reach, which makes the remainder apply where it does. Reading them as narrowing the duty or shifting the burden misses their role in fixing its reach.
questions.hint: Ask what the exceptions leave standing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collective guarantee that ran through a meeting
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a jointly given guarantee binds
questions.stem: Sheet 16 carries a note on a guarantee that several states entered into together at a single meeting.

options.text: Each guarantor is bound to the others as well as to the promise, since the obligation was made collectively.
Each guarantor is bound only to the promise, since the others' defaults do not touch it.
options.misconception: believes default by one does not affect the others

options.text: Only the first-named guarantor is bound, since the meeting named one state as answerable.
options.misconception: reads the naming of one state as sole liability

options.text: The guarantee is a political gesture, since a meeting cannot bind anyone in law.
options.misconception: denies that a collective act binds at all

questions.explanation: A joint guarantee creates obligations between the guarantors as well as toward the beneficiary, so one default is felt by the others. Being bound only to the promise misreads that.
questions.hint: Ask who owes what to whom.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling price and a rising duty on the same households
questions.learningObjective: Explain the double burden of a price fall and a duty rise
questions.stem: Sheet 17 sets out a note on households who saw the price of a staple fall while the duty on it rose in the same year.

answer.exemplar: A household that buys the staple pays the duty and the market price, so the two move against it in opposite ways. A falling price eases the cost of the grain itself while a rising duty takes a larger share of what the household earns to buy it. The two do not cancel, and neither figure tells the household what its cost will be without the other.

questions.explanation: The price paid and the duty borne on the same staple are separate claims on a household's income, and a fall in one does not undo a rise in the other. Taking either figure alone misstates the burden.
questions.hint: Ask what the household actually pays.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The machinery of a divided region
questions.learningObjective: Identify what an ordinance shows about a divided region

stimulus.body: The ordinance establishes a joint council composed of six members appointed by each of the two administrations, and gives it authority over customs receipts and over the shared fishery. It further provides that decisions of the council require the votes of five members from each side, and that a dispute over the fishery shall be carried to arbitration.

questions.stem: Sheet 18 asks the team to say what the ordinance shows.

options.text: It shows a single authority, since the council's decisions are binding on the whole region.
options.misconception: ignores the requirement of agreement

options.text: It shows a partition, since the region is administered by two separate sets of officers.
options.misconception: reads joint machinery as separation

options.text: It shows a shared machinery with vetoes, since neither side's votes alone carry a decision.
It shows no machinery at all, since the fishery dispute is sent to arbitration.
options.misconception: reads one tribunal as the absence of machinery

questions.explanation: The ordinance creates one body for both administrations, and requiring five votes from each side gives each a veto over the other's majority. A single authority or a partition misdescribes that.
questions.hint: Ask what the voting rule prevents.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A note whose deadline meets a timetable
questions.learningObjective: Determine how a deemed receipt rule starts a period

stimulus.body: A note states that the answer shall be given within forty days of the receipt of the request, and that the request shall be deemed received on the day it was handed to the courier. A postscript records that the courier took the road along the river, where the spring floods had washed out the bridge at the town.

questions.stem: Sheet 19 asks the team to say how the note's deadline operates.

options.text: The deadline is measured from the day the request was posted, since that is when it was sent.
options.misconception: measures the period from despatch

options.text: The deadline is suspended, since floods on the courier's road make the whole period impossible.
options.misconception: treats the delay as suspending the period

options.text: The deadline is shortened, since the courier's road is worse than the road the note assumed.
options.misconception: assumes difficulty shortens the period

options.text: The deadline runs from deemed receipt, which the note fixes as the day the request was handed over.

questions.explanation: The note itself fixes the starting point, deemed receipt on handover to the courier, and the period then runs from there. Delay on the road may excuse performance but does not move the fixed date.
questions.hint: Ask what the note calls the start.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Compare a blockade with the direct seizure of a port
questions.stem: Sheet 20 asks the team to compare a blockade with the direct seizure of a port.

options.text: A blockade works by interrupting supply and pressing the other side to yield, while seizure takes the port outright.
Both work in the same way, since a blockade is simply a seizure carried out at a distance.
options.misconception: collapses the two into one method

options.text: A blockade is the stronger measure, since it stops everything the port ever handled.
options.misconception: assumes a blockade stops all trade

options.text: Seizure is the stronger measure, since a blockade requires the other side to refuse to negotiate.
options.misconception: assumes a blockade needs refusal to negotiate

questions.explanation: A blockade is pressure applied to supply and leaves the port in the other side's hands, which is why terms can be pressed. Seizure removes the port, and a blockade stops nothing at once.
questions.hint: Ask what the port is left doing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Troops in a capital that has declared a republic
questions.learningObjective: Determine what foreign troops in a capital signify for a republic
questions.stem: Sheet 21 asks what follows from the presence of foreign troops in a capital where a republic has just been declared.

options.text: Nothing, since troops in a capital are always transient and the proclamation stands.
options.misconception: assumes transience settles standing

options.text: The proclamation may be read as backed, since the presence of the troops can signal recognition.
The republic is dissolved at once, since its capital is occupied by a foreign army.
options.misconception: treats occupation as dissolution

options.text: The capital becomes neutral ground, and the troops must withdraw beyond its walls.
options.misconception: invents a rule of withdrawal

questions.explanation: A proclamation asserts a new state, and foreign troops in the capital at that moment can be read as recognition of it. Their transience settles nothing about standing, and no rule requires their withdrawal.
questions.hint: Ask what a presence can be taken to mean.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: Design a method for finding the governing terms of a settlement
questions.stem: Sheet 22 asks for a method by which the team can establish which terms of a settlement actually governed.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the terms as first adopted, then look for any reopening of an article while the sitting was still open, and record the form in which each article was finally adopted. Where the record shows a reopened article, the later form governs the earlier; where it does not, the original stands. The chronology of adoption, not the order of the printed text, decides the matter.

questions.explanation: Which terms governed is a question of chronology, visible in the record of adoption and reopening. Assuming the earliest draft survived, or following the printed order, decides it by accident.
questions.hint: Follow the order of adoption.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Say what a pair of provisos does to an article

stimulus.body: Article 3 requires the two states to respect each other's merchant shipping and to open their ports in times of war. A proviso to the article provides that the obligation shall not extend to vessels carrying contraband, and that the first state may detain any such vessel entering its roads. A second proviso provides that nothing in the article shall be taken to prevent either state from searching vessels in its own harbour for the purpose of enforcing its own laws.

questions.stem: Sheet 23 asks the team to say what the provisos do.

options.text: They withdraw the article, since a proviso that limits an obligation ends it.
options.misconception: treats a proviso as a withdrawal

options.text: They transfer the obligation to the other state, since the first has excepted itself.
options.misconception: assumes exceptions transfer the duty

options.text: They create a second duty, since every proviso adds a new obligation in place of the first.
options.misconception: claims provisos always add duties

options.text: They mark where the duty does not reach and give the first state a separate power to detain.

questions.explanation: The first proviso removes contraband vessels from the opening obligation and gives the first state a power of detention; the second confirms each state's harbour jurisdiction. A proviso withdraws nothing.
questions.hint: Read each proviso on its own terms.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collective guarantee that ran through a meeting
questions.learningObjective: Say what a record of a joint guarantee establishes

stimulus.body: The record states that the three states entered into the guarantee at one sitting and that each of them engaged to stand surety for the others in the sum of two hundred thousand pounds, and that the obligation was to arise the moment any one of them defaulted. A rider records that the guarantor that pays is to be repaid out of the common fund, and that the shares of the common fund are to be set by a commission.

questions.stem: Sheet 24 asks the team to say what the record establishes.

options.text: The states are mutually liable, with the defaulting one triggering the whole obligation to pay.
Only the defaulting state is liable, since the others merely promise to recommend repayment later.
options.misconception: reduces the guarantee to a recommendation

options.text: No one is liable until a commission has set the shares, since the amounts are undetermined.
options.misconception: makes shares a precondition of liability

options.text: The obligation is divided equally and finally, since the commission has only one possible division.
options.misconception: assumes a single possible division

questions.explanation: Each state engaged to stand surety for the others and the obligation arose on any one default, so it is mutual and triggered. Setting the shares afterwards concerns reimbursement, not liability.
questions.hint: Ask what triggers the obligation.

questions.topic: A falling price and a rising duty on the same households
questions.learningObjective: Set out the effect on a household's cost of food
questions.stem: Sheet 25 asks the team to set out what happens to a household's cost of food when the price falls and the duty on the same food rises.

options.text: The cost falls, because the cheaper market price outweighs any increase in the duty charged.
options.misconception: assumes the price change outweighs the duty

options.text: The cost depends on both, because the household pays the market price and the duty on the same food.
The cost is unchanged, because a falling price and a rising duty were agreed in the same year.
options.misconception: assumes agreement in one year cancels out

options.text: The cost rises without limit, since a rising duty can be charged at any level on the staple.
options.misconception: assumes a duty may be set without limit

questions.explanation: A household pays both the market price and the duty, and only the two together give its cost, so a fall in one leaves the burden of the other intact. Cancellation misdescribes the pair.
questions.hint: Ask what the household pays twice.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The machinery of a divided region
questions.learningObjective: Identify what the machinery of a divided region is designed to achieve
questions.stem: Sheet 26 asks what the machinery of a divided region is designed to achieve.

options.text: To settle every dispute in the region, so that no question is left to arbitration later.
options.misconception: assumes the machinery eliminates all disputes

options.text: To separate the two administrations, so that each governs its own half without contact.
options.misconception: describes the machinery as separation

options.text: To give the two sides a shared forum in which each can block the other's majority decisions.
To speed up customs, since the fishery receipts were the real purpose of the council.
options.misconception: misses the blocking function entirely

questions.explanation: Joint machinery is built so that both administrations share a forum and neither can carry a decision the other will not accept. It does not settle everything or separate the two.
questions.hint: Ask what the voting rule is for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A note whose deadline meets a timetable
questions.learningObjective: Say how a period and a seasonal route interact

stimulus.kind: note in a file of correspondence
stimulus.body: The note asks that the answer be sent within thirty days of the date written at the head of the note, and that the answer travel by the northern post whenever the season permits. A footnote explains that the northern post is closed from the first frost until the thaw, and that the note was written on the tenth of the month.

questions.stem: Sheet 27 asks the team to say how the note's terms interact.

options.text: The thirty days runs only when the northern post is open, since the note makes the post the condition.
options.misconception: treats the route as a condition of the period

options.text: The thirty days runs from the thaw, since the post opens then and the note cannot be answered before.
options.misconception: moves the start to the thaw

options.text: The note has no date at all, because the season prevents the day from being certain.
options.misconception: denies the date because of the season

options.text: The thirty days runs from the written date, while the seasonal post is only the means of travel.

questions.explanation: The note fixes the period and names a route conditionally, so the period runs from the date written; the post governs only how the answer travels. A closed post delays performance without resetting the clock.
questions.hint: Ask what fixes the clock and what the post fixes.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Read an instruction to see what a blockade is designed to do

stimulus.body: The instruction directs that the squadron shall watch the approaches to the enemy's port and turn back merchant vessels bound there with cargo of war, while permitting passage to vessels carrying grain and ordinary goods. It adds that any vessel that ignores the direction shall be seized and brought before the prize court, and that the watch shall be kept night and day until further orders.

questions.stem: Sheet 28 asks the team to say what the instruction shows about the blockade's design.

options.text: It is designed to interrupt specified supply while letting ordinary trade continue, which keeps the pressure on.
It is designed to starve the port completely, since the instruction permits all goods to pass through.
options.misconception: reads the permission for grain as a general licence

options.text: It is designed to capture the port itself, since seizure of vessels is the first step toward taking it.
options.misconception: reads vessel seizure as a step to taking the port

options.text: It is designed to record the blockade rather than enforce it, since the watch is kept only by written order.
options.misconception: treats the instruction as documentary only

questions.explanation: The instruction selects what to stop and what to let through, which is how a blockade exerts pressure without starving a population. Seizing vessels that ignore the direction enforces the blockade.
questions.hint: Ask what the instruction lets through.

questions.stem: Sheet 29 asks the team to trace how the presence of troops in a capital can shape what a new republic is taken to be.

options.text: By occupying the council house, since control of the building gives control of the claim.
options.misconception: reduces the question to a building

options.text: By signalling that the government abroad accepts the new regime, so the republic gains standing.
By forcing the new government to govern with a garrison, which makes it dependent by law.
options.misconception: assumes dependence on a garrison follows by law

options.text: By showing that the proclamation was made under duress, which voids it from the start.
options.misconception: jumps to duress from the presence of troops

questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: State what a settlement is like when it revises its own terms
questions.stem: Sheet 30 asks what a settlement is like when it revises its own preliminary terms before the sitting closes.

options.text: It is void, since a settled article may never be reopened in the same session.
options.misconception: assumes articles are final on adoption

options.text: It is two settlements, since a reopened article creates a second binding text.
options.misconception: counts a revision as a second text

options.text: It is the amended text that governs, because the later adoption within the same sitting supersedes the earlier.
It is the earlier text that governs, since first adoption gives the article its authority.
options.misconception: makes first adoption the source of authority

questions.explanation: A sitting that remains open may reconsider its own articles, and the form adopted last within it is operative. That is a revision of one settlement, not a voiding and not a second text.
questions.hint: Ask which adoption came last.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Explain how exceptions can strengthen the obligation beside them
questions.stem: Sheet 31 asks for an explanation of how a clause's exceptions can strengthen the obligation they sit beside.

answer.exemplar: A clause that excepts named cases from a general duty shows how wide the duty otherwise is, and it makes the remaining cases more clearly binding rather than less. It also gives the parties a common understanding of the limit, so the duty is not fought over at its edges. The exception therefore does two things at once: it carves out what is not owed and it confirms how firmly the rest is.

questions.explanation: An exception marks the boundary of a duty and, by doing so, confirms the extent of what remains, which is why it can sharpen the obligation. It neither transfers the burden nor enlarges the duty.
questions.hint: Ask what the exception makes clearer.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collective guarantee that ran through a meeting
questions.learningObjective: Say what a pledge made together by several states establishes

stimulus.body: The text records that the four states, being met together at the city, engaged one to all that if any one of them were attacked the others would at once send their armies and their fleets, and that none would make peace separately. A note in the margin records that the city where they met had no part in the pledge, its walls being used only for the conference.

questions.stem: Sheet 32 asks the team to say what the pledge establishes.

options.text: A mutual undertaking binding each state to all the others, none being able to act alone.
A pledge between the states and the city, since the conference met inside the city's walls.
options.misconception: makes the host city a party

options.text: A unilateral undertaking, since only the first-named state bound itself to the rest.
options.misconception: reads the pledge as one-sided

options.text: No undertaking at all, since a meeting cannot bind states that meet only by accident.
options.misconception: denies that a meeting can bind

questions.explanation: The pledge is one to all: each state engages to the others and none may make peace separately, so the obligation is mutual and collective. The city provided a venue only.
questions.hint: Ask who made the pledge and who did not.

questions.topic: A falling price and a rising duty on the same households
questions.learningObjective: Read what a table of prices, duties and wages shows

stimulus.body: The table sets out for each of three years the price of a quarter of oats in the market, the rate of duty on oats in the same year, and the wages of a labourer at the harvest. The oats price falls in the second and third years while the duty rate rises in each, and the wage column is unchanged throughout.

questions.stem: Sheet 33 asks the team to say what the table shows about the households that buy oats.

options.text: That their cost of oats fell, because the market price is what they actually pay at the stall.
options.misconception: forgets the duty in the purchase price

options.text: That the price they pay rose or fell with both figures together, so the table alone does not settle it.
That the duty cancelled the price fall exactly, since both changed by the same amount.
options.misconception: assumes the two changes were equal

options.text: That nothing changed for them, since their wages did not move over the three years.
options.misconception: assumes unchanged wages fix their cost

questions.explanation: A household pays the market price plus the duty, so the two series must be read together, and the table does not say the changes were equal. Unchanged wages mean no rise in income to offset a higher duty.
questions.hint: Ask what the household's outlay consists of.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A note whose deadline meets a timetable
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a note fixes when it names both a period and a route
questions.stem: Sheet 35 asks what a note that names both a deadline and a means of delivery actually fixes.

options.text: It fixes the means alone, since a route named in a note is the part that will be remembered.
options.misconception: prioritises the route over the period

options.text: It fixes the date alone, since the means of delivery is a matter for the traveller.
options.misconception: treats the route as irrelevant to the obligation

options.text: It fixes neither, since a note is an expression of intention and binds nobody.
options.misconception: denies that a note binds at all

options.text: It fixes the period and the route, so the route may excuse delay but does not change the date.

questions.explanation: A note that names a period and a route fixes both, and they differ: the route is conditional, so difficulty may excuse delay without altering the date. Neither half cancels the other.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a blockade works as a method of coercion
questions.stem: Sheet 36 asks for an explanation of how a blockade works as a method of coercion.

answer.exemplar: A blockade substitutes the difficulty of supply for the difficulty of conquest. The blockading power makes the enemy's ordinary supply of food, fuel and money difficult, so that the government in the capital must choose between continuing the acts that caused the blockade and accepting terms; every day the supply continues, the pressure and the cost of refusing both grow. The aim is a decision, not a possession.

questions.explanation: A blockade works by making the alternative to yielding steadily more costly, so that a decision becomes preferable to endurance. It aims at the enemy's choice of policy, not at taking its territory.
questions.hint: Ask what the blockade makes expensive.

questions.topic: Troops in a capital that has declared a republic
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a report shows about the standing of a republic

stimulus.body: The report states that the government at home has instructed its minister to attend the ceremony in the capital and to take no part in it beyond the ordinary courtesies, and that the minister's attendance was not to be made the subject of any address. A footnote records that the detachment in the capital had been in the city for three weeks before the proclamation and that its commander had dined with the leading citizens.

options.text: It shows the republic is unrecognised, since the minister was forbidden to make an address.
options.misconception: reads a refusal to speak as non-recognition

options.text: It shows the presence may be read as recognition, though the report's wording leaves it unstated.
It shows the republic is dissolved, since foreign troops were in the capital before the proclamation.
options.misconception: reads prior presence as dissolution

options.text: It shows the republic was imposed by force, since the commander dined with the leading citizens.
options.misconception: reads a courtesy dinner as coercion

questions.explanation: A minister's attendance, with troops present and their commander received by the citizens, is conduct from which recognition may be read, though the report does not state it. The instructions' silence settles nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the report does not say.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: Say what a set of minutes shows about a settlement

stimulus.body: The minute records that the assembly opened by adopting a set of articles without division, and that on the second day the article concerning the fishery was withdrawn by its author, who stated that the question had been settled by the commission already sitting. options.misconception: equates one open article with total failure

options.text: It was replaced wholesale, since the commission's award took the place of the assembly's articles.
options.misconception: supposes the commission replaced everything

options.text: It stands with one article left to the commission's award, which the assembly agreed to enforce.
It was never adopted, since the opening adoption was provisional until the fishery article was settled.
options.misconception: makes the whole adoption provisional

questions.explanation: The minutes show a settlement whose fishery article was left, by agreement, to the commission sitting, and the assembly agreed to enforce the award. That is a deliberate allocation, not a failure.

questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Judge how exceptions affect the strength of a treaty
questions.stem: Sheet 39 asks the team to judge how exceptions in a treaty affect the strength of the treaty itself.

options.text: They weaken it, since every exception is a hole that the obligation can be slipped through.
options.misconception: treats each exception as a loophole

options.text: They leave it unchanged, since exceptions are only explanatory notes attached to the text.
options.misconception: treats exceptions as mere explanation

options.text: They transfer it, since a treaty with exceptions binds only those who asked for them.
options.misconception: believes exceptions change who is bound

options.text: They sharpen it, since they fix where the obligation applies and leave the rest standing firm.

questions.explanation: Exceptions fix the boundary of an obligation, and a known boundary is easier to enforce than an open one, so well-drawn exceptions can strengthen a treaty. Calling each a loophole misses their work.
questions.hint: Ask what a settled boundary is worth.

questions.learningObjective: Identify what a shared occasion adds to a guarantee
questions.stem: Sheet 40 asks what makes a guarantee given at a single meeting different from one given separately.

options.text: The states are bound to one another, so a default by one triggers the others' obligations directly.

options.misconception: confuses solemnity with legal effect

options.text: The guarantee is weaker, since a meeting shows the states had not consulted their own advisers.
options.misconception: reads a meeting as haste

options.text: The guarantee is void, since states may not act jointly upon one another's obligations.
options.misconception: claims joint action is forbidden

questions.explanation: What the meeting adds is the direct link between guarantors, so one default immediately engages the others, rather than separate promises. Solemnity and haste are not what it contributes.

questions.topic: A falling price and a rising duty on the same households
questions.learningObjective: Explain why both movements hit the same household
questions.stem: Sheet 41 asks for an explanation of why a falling price and a rising duty hit the same households twice over.

answer.exemplar: A household that eats oats pays two things for them: the miller's price and the state's duty, and the duty is levied on the grain as it enters the market, so it is already inside the price the household pays. When the market price falls and the duty rate rises in the same year, the household gains on one line and loses on another, and what it actually pays is the product of the two, not the more flattering of them.

questions.explanation: The duty is collected before the grain reaches the household and is embedded in the price, so the household meets both movements in one purchase. Reading either series alone misstates the cost.
questions.hint: Ask how the duty reaches the household.

stimulus.body: The rule book provides that the council shall consist of twelve members, six appointed by each administration, and that each member shall vote only on matters touching the constituency that appointed him. options.misconception: ignores the division of competence

options.text: It leaves the region without machinery, since appeals to a mediator show that the council cannot decide.
options.misconception: reads a mediator as an absence of machinery

options.text: It splits the council's work by constituency and puts shared subjects under a joint board.
It makes each administration responsible for everything, since members vote only for their own side.
options.misconception: confuses constituency rules with total separation

questions.explanation: The rule book divides the council's work by constituency and puts shared subjects under a joint board, with a mediator for questions of principle. That is divided competence, not concentration.

options.misconception: ignores the amendment to the standing order

options.text: By counting to the last day of the quarter, since a session ends with the quarter it begins in.
options.misconception: confuses the session's date with the quarter's end

options.text: By counting to the first day of the third month, since the note names the third month itself.
options.misconception: confuses the note's words with the standing order

options.text: By reference to the session as the standing order now fixes it, since the note does not name a month.

questions.explanation: The note refers to a session rather than a date, so the date comes from the standing order as it stands, which the footnote shows was moved. Counting to the original month substitutes another rule.

questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Weigh what a blockade achieves and what it leaves undone
questions.stem: Sheet 44 asks the team to weigh what a blockade achieves and what it leaves undone.

options.text: It forces the other side to weigh its course against the cost of continuing, which is pressure, not conquest.
It ends the war at once, since a closed port removes the enemy's ability to fight.
options.misconception: assumes a closed port ends a war

options.text: It changes nothing at all, since a blockade can always be run around by a neutral port.
options.misconception: believes blockades are easily evaded

options.text: It settles the dispute, since the terms of the blockade itself are the terms of peace.
options.misconception: treats the blockade terms as peace terms

questions.explanation: A blockade changes the calculation on the other side, which is its effect; it does not end a war by itself, cannot be assumed evaded, and carries no peace terms of its own.
questions.hint: Ask what the blockade changes on the other side.

questions.topic: Troops in a capital that has declared a republic
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of foreign troops on a republic declared there
questions.stem: Sheet 45 asks which statement best describes the effect of foreign troops in a capital on a republic declared there.

options.text: It nullifies the proclamation, since a republic declared before armed forces is no declaration.

options.text: It may lend the proclamation recognition, since the troops' presence can signify the outside power's consent.
It proves the republic was imposed, since no troops would be present without orders to compel.
options.misconception: treats presence as proof of compulsion

options.text: It leaves the republic exactly as it was, since a proclamation binds only those inside the walls.
options.misconception: believes declarations bind only the declarers

questions.explanation: Foreign troops in the capital can carry the sense that the outside power accepts the new regime, which is what recognition of a claim looks like in practice. Presence neither nullifies nor compels it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: State what a settlement's revision of its own terms means
questions.stem: Sheet 46 asks for a plain statement of what it means for a settlement to revise its own preliminary terms.

answer.exemplar: It means the body that adopted the terms was still sitting and chose to look again, so the terms it first adopted were drafts rather than a closed bargain. Where it reopened an article and adopted it in a different form, that later form is the settlement, and the earlier one is a step in the making of it. Nothing is void and no second settlement is created.

questions.explanation: Revision of one's own preliminary terms shows that the first adoption was provisional within an open sitting, and the later form governs. It is neither a voiding nor the birth of a second settlement.

questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Say what a proviso does to a duty and to payment

stimulus.body: The regulation requires that every cargo landing at the port be entered in the register within three days of the landing and that the duty be paid on entry. questions.stem: Sheet 47 asks the team to say what the proviso does.

options.text: It removes the duty for bonded vessels, since a bond replaces the entry and the payment.
options.misconception: confuses a deferred duty with an exempt one

options.text: It binds every vessel, since a general regulation applies even where a proviso exists.
options.misconception: ignores the presence of the proviso

options.text: It creates a second duty for bonded masters, since the bond adds an obligation of its own.
options.misconception: claims the bond creates an extra duty

options.text: It suspends the entry requirement for bonded masters while leaving the duty payable on discharge.

questions.explanation: The proviso excuses bonded masters from the three-day entry rule until the bond is discharged, when the full duty falls due. A bond defers payment rather than remitting it.

questions.topic: A collective guarantee that ran through a meeting
questions.learningObjective: Say what a resolution on mutual defence provides

stimulus.body: The resolution states that the five states, being represented at the same congress, engage mutually that should the integrity of any one of them be attacked, the others will in common defend it, and that no one of them will conclude a separate peace. questions.stem: Sheet 48 asks the team to say what the resolution provides.

options.text: A mutual defence engagement with a majority rule, where three of the five may bind the rest.
A single undertaking by the congress as a body, since only the congress can bind a state.
options.misconception: makes the congress itself the promisor

options.text: A promise of consultation, since the reference to defending shows the states meant only to advise.
options.misconception: softens a defence pledge into advice

options.text: An agreement that dies with the congress, since nothing can bind after the meeting closes.
options.misconception: assumes the binding force ends with the meeting

questions.explanation: The resolution engages the states mutually, makes a majority of three decisive for all, and forbids a separate peace. Treating it as advice or as dead on the closing day misreads it.

options.text: The first position is better, since a falling price always outweighs a rising duty.
options.misconception: assumes the price fall outweighs the duty rise

options.text: Both must be measured on the outlay, because the price and the duty are separate claims on the same income.
The first position is worse, since a falling price shows the market is turning against the household.
options.misconception: reads a market fall as evidence of household hardship

options.text: The two positions are identical, since the household's income is the same in both cases.
options.misconception: assumes income alone settles the comparison

questions.topic: The machinery of a divided region

options.text: Two governments acting independently, with the earlier customs arrangement continuing in practice.
options.misconception: describes parallel machinery as independent action

options.text: One government in all but name, since the joint council's decisions are executed by one side.

A temporary arrangement with no rules of its own, since everything is left to the two governments.
options.misconception: denies that the machinery has rules

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a note can fix a deadline the timetable makes awkward
questions.stem: Sheet 51 asks for an explanation of how a note can fix a deadline that the parties' timetable may make awkward.

answer.exemplar: A note can fix its own deadline by naming a period that runs from a defined event, or by referring to a session or a return that the standing arrangements fix on a particular day. In either case the note does not need to know what the timetable will do: it borrows the timetable's dates. Where a note names neither, it cannot fix a date, and the parties are left with whatever the general law supplies.

questions.explanation: A note fixes a deadline either by naming a period from a defined event or by borrowing the date of a session the standing arrangements fix. Naming neither leaves the date to the general law.

questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Say what an admiralty paper shows about a blockade's purpose

stimulus.body: The paper sets out the objects of the blockade, namely to prevent the arrival at the enemy's port of arms, powder and stores of war, and to compel the enemy's government to consent to terms already offered. questions.stem: Sheet 52 asks the team to say what the paper shows about the blockade's purpose.

It is a measure of total starvation, since the paper's list of goods is the whole of its concern.
options.misconception: reads the listed goods as the whole concern

options.text: It is a measure of conquest, since examining cargo is the ordinary form of preparing an assault.
options.misconception: reads examination as a step to assault

options.text: It is a measure of revenue, since detaining vessels lets the prize court take a share of the cargo.
options.misconception: treats prize as the purpose of the blockade

questions.explanation: The paper names its objects: to stop war stores and to obtain consent to terms already offered, with grain and salt allowed through. Taking prize from detained vessels is a consequence, not the purpose.

questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the work an exception does to a rule
questions.stem: Sheet 55 asks which statement best describes the work done by an exception to a general rule.

options.text: It cancels the rule for every case, since an exception is the opposite of a rule.
options.misconception: treats an exception as cancelling the rule

options.text: It changes the rule's wording, since exceptions are drafted into the text itself.
options.misconception: claims exceptions rewrite the rule

options.text: It creates a new rule for the excepted cases, since exceptions need their own obligations.
options.misconception: says exceptions create fresh obligations

options.text: It marks where the rule does not reach, which fixes the rule's extent and leaves the rest standing.

questions.explanation: An exception defines the boundary of a rule, and that boundary makes the remainder clearer and firmer rather than weaker. It does not cancel the rule, rewrite its words, or introduce fresh duties.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collective guarantee that ran through a meeting
questions.learningObjective: Account for the two stages of a collective guarantee
questions.stem: Sheet 56 asks for an account of how a collective guarantee made at a meeting operates between the guarantors.

answer.exemplar: Each guarantor owes the beneficiary the whole of the sum it guaranteed, so that a default by one obliges the others to pay without waiting for an assessment of what each owes. The obligation between the guarantors is a second one, created by the same act: whoever pays is entitled to reimbursement from the others, and the shares are settled afterwards by a commission. Mutual liability and reimbursement are therefore two separate stages.

questions.explanation: A collective guarantee has two stages, joint liability to the beneficiary and reimbursement between guarantors, and the second settles shares only after the first is performed.

options.text: They show the price was irrelevant, since the duty had already been collected at the market.
options.misconception: concludes price is irrelevant to the buyer

questions.explanation: The returns show eight households buying fewer quarters in the year the price fell and the duty rose, which is what a tightening budget looks like. It does not show which movement caused it.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Recall what a blockade is built to do
questions.stem: Sheet 60 asks what a blockade is built to do, in the plainest terms.

options.text: To make the supply of the other side difficult enough that it must choose to yield.
To take the enemy's port and hold it, since a port commands the coast around it.
options.misconception: reduces the blockade to taking a port

options.text: To hurt the traders who carry goods, since merchants are easier to intimidate than governments.
options.misconception: makes merchants the blockade's real target

options.text: To close the sea to all shipping, since a partial measure produces no pressure at all.
options.misconception: assumes only a total closure has effect

questions.explanation: A blockade exists to make continued resistance more costly than acceptance, and it is deliberately partial, since total closure would destroy the trade it uses as leverage. Taking a port is another operation.
questions.hint: Ask what it makes more costly.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Troops in a capital that has declared a republic
questions.learningObjective: Explain why foreign troops in a capital matter to a republic
questions.stem: Sheet 61 asks for an explanation of why foreign troops in a capital can matter to a republic proclaimed there.

answer.exemplar: A proclamation is a claim, and the recognition of other states is what turns a claim into a standing position. Troops stationed in the capital are one of the few visible ways in which the outside power's attitude can be demonstrated, and their presence, without any declaration, can be read by others as an indication that the new regime is accepted. It is an indication, not a formal act, and much turns on how the troops behave.

questions.explanation: Recognition gives a claim standing, and another state's troops in the capital are one of the few visible ways an attitude can be shown without words. It is an indication, not a formal act.
questions.hint: Ask what recognition does for a claim.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: Say what a circulated draft with corrections shows

stimulus.body: The draft bears the words first read on the third day, and a later hand has entered against the fourth article the words withdrawn, together with a reference to the commission's award. A note on the cover states that the draft was circulated in advance and that objections were to be sent to the secretary before the day of the sitting.

questions.stem: Sheet 62 asks the team to say what the draft shows about the settlement's terms.

options.text: That the fourth article was void, since an article withdrawn before adoption was never in the settlement.
options.misconception: equates withdrawal with voiding

options.text: That the draft was final, since corrections were entered on it after it was circulated.
options.misconception: treats a circulated draft as final

options.text: That the terms were still open when circulated, and one article was later left to the commission.
That objections had already been decided, since the secretary had recorded the withdrawal.
options.misconception: assumes recorded objections were decided

questions.explanation: The draft was circulated for objection before the sitting, so the terms were open then, and the withdrawal entered against the fourth article leaves it to the commission. A circulated draft is not final.
questions.hint: Ask when objections were due.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The exceptions that create an obligation
questions.learningObjective: Say what an article with a schedule of classes does

stimulus.body: Article 6 provides that the two states shall guarantee each other against the loss of the territory held in common, and that the guarantee shall hold against every claim to that territory however made. A schedule lists three classes of claim, and the article adds that a claim made under any other class shall not affect the guarantee, and that the two states shall settle the question of the class of a claim before acting upon it.

questions.stem: Sheet 63 asks the team to say what the article does.

options.text: It limits the guarantee to claims of the three listed classes, which is what a schedule of exceptions means.
options.misconception: reads the schedule as limiting the guarantee

options.text: It withdraws the guarantee, since the schedule shows that no claim could be answered.
options.misconception: reads a schedule as a withdrawal

options.text: It makes the guarantee automatic, since the class of a claim is settled by the list without inquiry.
options.misconception: removes the requirement to settle the class

options.text: It makes the guarantee conditional on the class of claim, which the parties must settle before acting.

questions.explanation: The guarantee holds against every claim however made, and the schedule carves out claims of other classes, which the parties must classify before acting. A carve-out neither withdraws the guarantee nor makes it automatic.
questions.hint: Ask what happens before the parties act.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A collective guarantee that ran through a meeting
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a collective guarantee differs from separate promises
questions.stem: Sheet 64 asks the team to set out how a collective guarantee differs from a series of separate promises.

options.text: One default engages all the guarantors at once, and each can be called on for the whole sum.
Each guarantor remains answerable only for its own share, since the promises were made separately.
options.misconception: reads a joint pledge as separate liability

options.text: The guarantors may agree among themselves to substitute another guarantor, since they acted together.
options.misconception: assumes the group may replace a guarantor

options.text: The obligation disappears if the least of the guarantors fails, since the others may disclaim the whole.
options.misconception: allows a disclaimer of the whole pledge

questions.explanation: A collective guarantee means one default engages every guarantor for the whole sum, with reimbursement settled afterwards, which separate promises would not give. Shares and disclaimers are not features of a joint pledge.
questions.hint: Ask what one default sets off.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A falling price and a rising duty on the same households
questions.learningObjective: State what follows from a price fall and a duty rise together
questions.stem: Sheet 65 asks what follows when the price of a staple falls and the duty on it rises in the same year.

options.text: Households pay less, since the market price is the part of the cost they can see.
options.misconception: ignores the duty in the visible cost

options.text: Households pay the two together, so the net effect has to be worked out on the whole outlay.
Households pay more, since a rising duty always outweighs a falling price for a buyer.
options.misconception: assumes the duty rise always outweighs the price fall

options.text: Households pay exactly as before, since one movement cancels the other by design.
options.misconception: assumes designed cancellation

questions.explanation: The household's outlay is the price plus the duty, so the two movements must be combined before anything is said about it. A falling price is not the whole of the cost, and nothing cancels a duty rise.
questions.hint: Ask what the outlay consists of.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The machinery of a divided region
questions.learningObjective: Analyse why the machinery gives each side a veto
questions.stem: Sheet 66 asks for an analysis of why the machinery of a divided region is built to give each side a veto.

answer.exemplar: Each administration of a divided region holds things it would lose if the other could decide alone, whether a fishery, a customs arrangement or a road. A machinery that allowed a bare majority to carry a question would put those things at the mercy of the other side's numbers, which no division of a country can be asked to accept. Parity and the requirement of agreement give each side a share in the decision and a hold on it, which is what makes a single authority acceptable.

questions.explanation: The veto exists because each side holds interests it would lose to a bare majority of the other, so parity and agreement make a shared authority tolerable. A machinery without them is a transfer of control.
questions.hint: Ask what each side would lose.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A note whose deadline meets a timetable
questions.learningObjective: Identify which sitting a note refers to

stimulus.body: The schedule lists the sittings of the year, giving for each the date of its opening, and states that where a term of days is reckoned from the opening of a sitting it shall count from the first day of the second month. A note in the margin records that the sitting named in the correspondence was the one held in the fourth month, and that the parties meant the earlier sitting in the third month.

questions.stem: Sheet 67 asks the team to say which sitting the note refers to.

options.text: The sitting of the fourth month, since the note is later in date than the correspondence.
options.misconception: picks the later sitting on a date

options.text: The sitting of the third month, since the note is later than the correspondence.
options.misconception: picks the earlier sitting on a date

options.text: Neither, since the parties meant a sitting that the schedule does not list.
options.misconception: assumes an unlisted sitting

options.text: The sitting the parties meant, as recorded in the margin, rather than the one the schedule first suggests.

questions.explanation: The margin records what the parties meant, and the schedule fixes only how a term is reckoned once a sitting is identified. Choosing by the date of the note ignores that record.
questions.hint: Ask what the margin records.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a blockade is built to do
questions.learningObjective: Read what a port report shows about the blockade's working

stimulus.body: The officer reports that six vessels a week had entered the port before the watch was established and that four had entered since, of which two carried grain and two carried timber. He adds that the traders of the neighbouring town have petitioned to be allowed to bring salt without search, and that the request has been referred to the admiral.

questions.stem: Sheet 68 asks the team to say what the report shows about the blockade's working.

options.text: It narrows rather than closes the traffic, since some goods still pass and a petition is still possible.
It closes the port entirely, since traffic has fallen to four vessels a week.
options.misconception: reads a fall as a total closure

options.text: It has no effect at all, since four vessels still enter each week without search.
options.misconception: counts residual traffic as no effect

options.text: It has succeeded, since the traders now ask to be searched rather than to trade freely.
options.misconception: reads a petition as the goal achieved

questions.explanation: The figures show traffic reduced but not stopped, and the petition shows the blockade is administered by a choice about what passes, not by a closed port. Falling numbers alone are not closure.
questions.hint: Ask what the traffic figures show and do not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Troops in a capital that has declared a republic
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a republic came to be recognised
questions.stem: Sheet 69 asks the team to set out how a republic declared in a capital with foreign troops came to be recognised.

options.text: By the troops' presence alone, since recognition needs nothing more than a visible sign of favour.
options.misconception: treats a visible sign as recognition

options.text: By conduct sustained after the proclamation, which others read as the outside power's acceptance.
By the wording of the proclamation itself, which was drafted to invite recognition.
options.misconception: credits wording rather than conduct

options.text: By the troops' withdrawal, since leaving the capital showed the republic was not supported.
options.misconception: reads withdrawal as a recognition event

questions.explanation: Recognition comes from the continued conduct of the power that could recognise, read by others as acceptance of the new regime, so wording alone does not carry it. Withdrawal is not acceptance.
questions.hint: Ask what others could read into the conduct.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A settlement that revised its own preliminary terms
questions.learningObjective: State what a settlement with revised preliminary terms amounts to
questions.stem: Sheet 70 asks what a settlement whose own preliminary terms were revised before the sitting closed amounts to.

options.text: A void agreement, since terms that change cannot bind the parties who agreed them.
options.misconception: makes revision void the agreement

options.text: Two agreements, since the first adoption and the later one each need their own consent.
options.misconception: counts each adoption as a separate consent

options.text: One agreement in the course of being made, whose later form governs the earlier.
A draft only, since the revision shows the parties had never reached agreement at all.
options.misconception: reads revision as proof of no agreement

questions.explanation: A settlement that revises its preliminary terms is one agreement in the course of being made, and the later form governs. It is neither void, nor two agreements needing separate consents, nor a mere draft.
questions.hint: Ask what the revision shows about the agreement.
